title: AI drafts, a person decides
dek: What running support for a store shipping to 61 countries taught me about using AI at work.
body:
Until November 2026 I ran operations and customer service for Aubrica, an online store shipping posture and wellness products to 61 countries. Every order passed through four systems: Shopify for the order and its tags, the fulfilment partner for the pick and the cost, a carrier for the parcel and a support inbox for what the customer had said. Knowing what to do next meant opening all four.

Replies depended on who was answering, and nothing showed how the business was running as a whole. That's the kind of problem people now expect AI to fix on its own. I don't think it can, and I don't think it should.

## Write the process down first

Before any AI touched a reply, I wrote the support process down: replies within one business day, the same day for cancellations, refunds and urgent shipping, a template for every common case, and country-by-country rules for holding orders with missing details. It's not glamorous, but without it AI would only have produced inconsistency faster.

Then I built the Order Tracker around that process. It syncs Shopify and 17TRACK carrier tracking, puts every active order in one queue and says what each one needs next: escalate to the owner, needs a phone number, needs a customs ID, tracking stalled. The first import held 1,550 orders.

## Where the AI sits

AI drafted the routine replies from those templates and turned long support notes into a one-line next action. A person read every reply before it went. That was the rule, and it was the right one.

> AI drafted the routine replies. A person read every reply before it went.

The drafts were mostly good, but a draft can be confidently wrong, or polite in a way that misses what an upset customer is actually asking. Reading every one took minutes. Getting one wrong could cost a customer's trust, and that's much harder to win back.

## The time goes somewhere better

What AI really gave us was time. The routine replies took less of it, so more went on the orders that needed a decision and the customers who needed a person. That's the version of AI at work I believe in: it handles the repetitive parts, it's honest about being a draft, and someone stays accountable for what goes out.

I think a lot about how AI is being rolled out right now, and how often accountability gets designed out to save a few minutes. My view is simple: if a message goes out in your name, a person should have read it. Build the process so that's easy, and AI becomes genuinely useful instead of quietly risky.
